units.title: Ethereum mainnet reference and cross-chain deployment parity
angles: Arithmetic and control flow. Read the interpreter this network runs at the release its endpoint reports, and any compiler, bytecode rewriting, caching or code analysis stage in front of it. Cover the 256 bit integer library and its pinned version, MULMOD, ADDMOD, DIV, SDIV, MOD, SMOD, SIGNEXTEND, SAR, SHL, SHR, BYTE, EXP, the comparisons, JUMP and JUMPI with the jump destination analysis, KECCAK256, MCOPY, memory expansion and CALLDATALOAD. Compare each with the Ethereum specification at the edges that OPCODES.md lists, and read the release notes and fix commits since the versions OPCODES.md records. Then rerun the scripts in research/network-risk/tools/opdiff (battery.py, targeted.py, pmdiff.py, pmdiff2.py, swaps.py, replay.py) for this unit's chain ids, write the outputs into your work directory, and add vectors for anything the reading makes suspicious. Report every result that differs from the specification, every release that changed these paths, how a wrong result would change the pool math in src/libraries (TickMath, BitMath, FullMath, SqrtPriceMath, SwapMath, TickBitmap) or the logic that depends on it, and which validators could run a different code path than the public endpoint.

Upcoming forks. Assume every network upgrade scheduled or proposed for the next six months ships. What changes for the PoolManager and for funds already inside it, and what could an ordinary account do the day after?

Most Rust clients among the 21 networks compute 256 bit arithmetic with the ruint crate, at different releases: 1.18.0 and 1.19.0 (older revm lines, MegaETH), 1.20.0 (Celo's next build), 1.20.1 (nanoreth nb-20261125-2 for HyperEVM) and 1.21.1 (Tempo and Ethereum's reth through evm2). The main branch changelog (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/recmo/uint/main/CHANGELOG.md) lists #634, which reimplements shifts by primitive integer types without truncating large amounts, #681, the mul_mod fix shipped as 1.21.1, and under Unreleased #701 and #704, a wrong wrapping_from result for negative integers narrower than the Uint. Task 1: fetch the crate sources of 1.18.0, 1.19.0, 1.20.0, 1.20.1 and 1.21.1 from static.crates.io into dl/ and say for each of #634, #681, #701 and #704 which releases contain the fault and which the fix, by reading the code. Task 2: list which ruint functions the instruction handlers the PoolManager build executes actually call (ADD, MUL, SUB, DIV, SDIV, MOD, SMOD, ADDMOD, MULMOD, EXP, SIGNEXTEND, LT, GT, SLT, SGT, EQ, ISZERO, AND, OR, XOR, NOT, BYTE, SHL, SHR, SAR, and the conversions used for memory offsets, jump targets, gas and CALL arguments) in revm-interpreter 35 to 43 as pinned by the clients, in mega-evm v1.7.4 and in evm2 35aa3280. For each say which release each network runs (research/network-risk/OPCODES.md has the client table) and whether a faulty function is on the path. Pay attention to conversions from Uint to usize or u64 and back (as_limbs, saturating_to, wrapping_to, try_from, wrapping_from), since a wrong narrow conversion changes memory offsets and jump targets, not arithmetic words. Task 3: build each of the five releases natively with the cargo that is present (crate source only, no toolchain download) and run one differential harness against a Python big integer reference: shifts by amounts 0 to 300, 2^32 and 2^64 for every primitive amount type, mul_mod, add_mod, div_rem, pow and the conversions of task 2, at least one million cases per function per release with a fixed seed, and plant one fault to show the harness catches it. Task 4: send the vectors that exercise any function found faulty in some release to every network through eth_call, with web3_clientVersion in the same batch, using the battery runner in research/network-risk/tools/opdiff as a model. Report a finding only if a network's answer differs from the specification.

Twenty cycles have compared the build's behaviour with the specification on 21 networks and found no difference an ordinary account can use, and the weakness the organisers planted is still not identified. This theme asks for an independent list made from the source alone. For this unit the order of reading differs from the general instructions above: do not read OPCODES.md, ASSUMPTIONS.md or earlier research files first. Read SCHEMA.md for the output format and nothing else from the review until Step 3. Step 1, before opening research/network-risk/OPCODES.md, REPORT.md, FINDINGS.md, CLEARED.md or anything under research/network-risk/state except networks.json and research/network-risk/cycles: read every file under src/ in full (PoolManager.sol, the libraries, the types, ERC6909.sol, Extsload.sol, Exttload.sol, NoDelegateCall.sol, ProtocolFees.sol) and write to your work directory a file assumptions.md that lists every assumption the code makes about the chain it runs on. Be concrete and cite file and line: what each opcode used in an assembly block must return (list each assembly block), what transient storage must do across calls, reverts and transactions, what a call to an address without code returns, how much gas a call forwards and what happens at the 63/64 rule, what msg.value and address(this).balance mean, how addresses are derived and which address bits carry meaning (hook permission flags in the low 14 bits of the hook address, src/libraries/Hooks.sol), what returndatasize and returndatacopy do after each call shape, how the chain id, block time, block number, coinbase, base fee or gas price are used or not used, what code size and code hash checks assume, how custom errors are bubbled, what memory is assumed clean or dirty, and which arithmetic relies on wrapping or on a revert. Step 2: for each assumption name which of the 21 networks in research/network-risk/state/networks.json you would expect, from general knowledge of that network's design, to be most likely to break it, and how an ordinary account could turn the break into a freeze or a loss for other users. Rank the list by how plausible and how damaging each is. Step 3: only now open OPCODES.md, FINDINGS.md and CLEARED.md and, for each of your top fifteen items, say whether the review tested it, with what evidence, and whether that evidence actually exercises your scenario or only something near it. Step 4: for the three highest-ranked items that the review tested weakly or not at all, test them yourself by read-only RPC with state overrides at the real PoolManager address on the networks concerned (the script builders in research/network-risk/tools/opdiff can be reused), and report what you find. Report a finding for anything an ordinary account can use; report every weakly tested item as a lead with the exact test that would settle it. Do not report items the review has already settled with direct evidence.
